newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: British fund says 1997 good for Sri Lanka tea.
newsitem.headline: British fund says 1997 good for Sri Lanka tea.

text.p: Sri Lankan tea prices should remain firm this year on steady demand due to a shortfall in world production, an official of Tea Plantations Investment Trust Plc (TPIT) said on Thursday.

"Tea production in Georgia in the CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States), which used to produce about 120-130 million kilograms a year, has disappeared with the collapse of the Soviet Union," Colin Kingsnorth, director and fund manager of TPIT told Reuters in Colombo.
Kingsnorth said a population explosion in India, which is converting that country into a net importer of tea, and a drought in Kenya , another major tea producer, will add to the shortfall.
In 1992, the Sri Lankan government privatised management of 23 regional plantation companies which own some 600,000 hectares of tea, rubber and coconut.
In late 1995 ownership of the plantation companies was privatised by selling 51 percent of each to a strategic investor and 20 percent on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE).
Ten percent is reserved for workers and the government retains the balance.
Six firms -- Bogawantalawa Plantations, Kotagala Plantations, Agalwatte Plantations, Kegalle Plantations, Horana Plantations, Kelani Valley Plantations -- are already listed on the CSE.
Strategic investors have bought stakes in seven more firms and they are due to be floated later this year.

Ten firms for which the process is yet to begin are due to see strategic holdings divested between April and June, said an official of the Public Enterprise Reform Commission, which oversees privatisations.
"We intend bidding for the strategic holding in three of the firms which are due to come out in April/May," Kingsnorth said.
Since foreigners are only permitted to hold up to 49 percent of the equity in a privatised plantation firm, TPIT will bid in concert with a Sri Lankan partner.

TPIT has raised $10 million on the London Stock Exchange to invest in Sri Lankan plantations set to be privatised. The trust is managed by Regent Fund Management (U.K.) which also manages the Regent Sri Lanka Fund.
Kingsnorth said he was bullish on the sector's growth prospects given the value added by private managers.

"With every private management company either developing CTC (crush tea curl) tea for bags, green tea or concentrate for canned tea, we should see share prices of listed tea firms moving up (by) three to four times in the next two to three years."

Local analysts said tea prices will come off last year's record highs but 1997 should still be a good year due to continuing demand from former Soviet republics and the Middle East, which favour Sri Lanka's low-grown orthodox teas.
The Colombo auction average for calendar 1996 rose to a record 103.88 rupees ($1.81) per kg from 72.21 rupees in 1995.
"We are optimistic about 1997 but do not see the runaway prices of 1996 due to better supply of tea," said Anil Cooke, a director at tea brokerage Forbes & Walker.
High prices in 1996 were partly due to supply being affected by a severe drought in Sri Lanka.
